1:
Two silences end at once, and Gill and Henry account for them differently. Gill reads the opening phrase as the breaking of a long silence: Job had spoken after the first trial to bless the name of the Lord and after the second to reprove his wife, but through the seven days he and his friends said nothing, and he began only when he saw they would not, his distemper perhaps having abated. Henry makes the silence itself the cause of what follows. Job's heart had long been hot within him, and while he was musing the fire burned, and burned the more for being stifled; the friends were afraid to speak lest they grieve him and he lest he offend them; they had come to comfort him but, finding his affliction so far out of the common, began to suspect him a hypocrite and to think comfort did not belong to him. Losers, Henry adds drily, think they may have leave to speak.

Gill notes that the second verse says answered although nobody had spoken to him, and takes it with one commentator that he answered his own calamity and their silence, while an older authority renders it simply that he cried out. Keil and Delitzsch treat the same verse as a problem in accentuation, three words separated so as to force an unusual pointing on the verb, and gloss it as beginning to speak on some previous incitement rather than replying to anything.

Where the poetry starts is disputed. Clarke draws the line here: there is nothing in the preceding chapters either in the form or the spirit of Hebrew poetry, and though it is easy to break narrative into half-lines, that does not make it verse; Asiatic poets commonly open with prose and only then begin the poem, which he takes to be the plan here. He grants his opponents their opinion in a sentence that concedes nothing: they have his consent while he takes the liberty of believing most decidedly the opposite. Gill agrees that the metre begins here but is candid that the metre itself is now pretty much unknown even to the Jews, and reports the opinion that the speeches were not delivered in verse but put into that form afterwards by the writer, adding that one Targum has not that Job spoke but that he sang. Keil and Delitzsch report the division modern critics make, a delirious cursing of life, an eager longing for death, and a reproachful inquiry after the end of such a life, then deny these are strophes at all while refusing the further claim that the book has no strophic structure anywhere.

Ellicott raises a question of priority none of the others touch. The resemblance between this chapter and a lament in Jeremiah is so close that one must be borrowed from the other, and he holds this the original: the chapter is indispensable to the poem here, whereas in the prophet it occurs casually, as the record of a passing mood, and reads like a man quoting a familiar writing much as he might quote a psalm.

Whether the curse can be excused divides the two who raise it. Henry allows that the extremity of the trouble may excuse it in part, and observes that where other men keep their birthday with rejoicing this man reckoned it the unhappiest day of his year, being the inlet to all his woe. Wesley refuses the excuse, since Job is afterwards reproved by God and accuses himself; he allows that Job stops short of cursing God and so makes the devil a liar, but holds that he reflects on providence indirectly, and calls the curse sinful on two counts, that it was vain, being spent on a thing incapable of blessing or cursing, and that it laid blame on God for giving him life that day.
3:
What is being cursed has to be settled before anything else. Gill allows both readings, the identical day on which Job was born, which amounts to wishing he had never been born, or the birthday as it came round yearly; on the first the wish is impossible and Job knew it, the design being to show the greatness of the affliction rather than to obtain anything. Keil and Delitzsch decide against a named opponent: the curse falls on the birth-day and the night of conception as they recur yearly, not on the actual first day. Clarke settles a smaller point the same way: though the word properly means conceived it should here be taken of birth, since it is most unlikely that the night of conception should be known or published.

The darkness asked for is meant literally. Gill is explicit that this is not the figurative darkness of calamity but gross natural darkness, the reverse of the word that made light. Clarke reduces the imprecation to a phrase, that the day be blotted out of the calendar, and sharpens it by remembering what the day had been, the birthday of a man once celebrated for his possessions and piety. Ellicott glosses the verb about God's regarding it as literally to require or ask for, and so to show care about.

The verb behind stain is read three ways. Ellicott takes it literally as redeem, so that darkness and the shadow of death claim the day as their rightful inheritance, and Gill reports the same rendering, that they challenge it as their own and leave light no share in it. Clarke goes to the root that gives the kinsman-redeemer, whose office was to buy back an inheritance and avenge a death, and makes the sense pursuit rather than possession: let the day be overtaken as the avenger of blood overtakes the offender.

On the night being struck from the calendar, Ellicott prefers let it not rejoice among the days of the year, as one of a glorious procession of nights. Clarke gives the Targum's version, that it be reckoned among no annual festival and computed in no month, notes that some take the word for a dark storm, and points out what governs the passage, that everything in it is personified, day and night and darkness and cloud alike. Wesley makes the same observation on the stars, that sense is ascribed to the night by a poetical fiction usual in all writers; and Ellicott supplies the phrase that shows it best, the eyelids of the dawn.

The word rendered solitary Clarke traces to Arabic, from a root meaning to cut off or lay bare, which also yields words for a rock and a burden; his gloss is that the night should be as destitute of good as a bare rock is of verdure. Gill fills in what such a night lacks, the journeys and business, the meetings of friends after the day's work, the feasts usual at night and at marriages, so that the silence should be as deep as if every creature were dead.

The verse about those who curse the day defeats them. Clarke says the English is scarcely intelligible and that he has waded through many interpretations without arriving at a probable notion; he reports the view that professional cursers are meant and rejects it, since a man who knew God's government as Job did would not have appealed to them. Ellicott offers the reading Clarke could not find, that those who pronounce days unlucky should treat this one as the standard, and notes that they are further described as ready to rouse leviathan, which is to say as desperate as that. Gill names among the candidates a people near Arabia said to curse the sun at its rising. Wesley keeps it simple, that men cursing their own birthday should spare a curse for his.
11:
Clarke separates three wishes where the English runs them together: dying in the womb without coming to maturity, being born dead without drawing breath, and dying shortly after birth; all three are meant, and the verses following take them in turn. Gill presses the first, that since conception was not prevented he wishes at least to have died before coming out alive. Henry watches the argument rather than the grammar and dislikes where it goes. Job, reflecting on the folly of wishing he had never been born, tries to mend it with something little better; and though a saying about the barren womb is allowed elsewhere, blessing the barren womb is one thing and cursing the fruitful womb another. His rule is brief: it is good to make the best of afflictions, but not to make the worst of mercies.

The knees and the breasts are taken as ordinary midwifery. Gill identifies the knees as the midwife's rather than the mother's, or possibly the father's, since it was the custom to take a newborn on the knee in acknowledgement; the complaint, on his reading, is that Job was caught instead of left to fall. Ellicott puts it in one sentence, asking why he was nursed with care instead of being allowed to fall to the ground and be killed. Wesley expands the complaint and turns on it: the nurse's laying him on her knees rather than the bare ground is what he calls their cruel kindness; then he records his verdict, that Job is here unthankfully despising the wonderful mercies of God toward helpless infants.

What death would have offered is described by all of them as rest. Gill makes the grave to the dead what a bed is to the living, a place of ease free from care and thought, and better than a bed, since on a bed there is often tossing to and fro and in the grave none. Clarke runs through the verbs in order: insensible, quiet, asleep and unconscious of evil, at rest beyond the reach of calamity. Keil and Delitzsch state the principle the passage turns on, that there all enjoy the rest they could not find here, the troublers and the troubled alike.

The company Job would have kept is read two ways. Gill offers first that he might have been buried with kings as his own ancestors, being a man of distinction, then prefers the levelling sense, that death spares neither the power of kings nor the wisdom of counsellors, and that after it a child who died at birth stands equal with them. Clarke defines the counsellors as the privy advisers without whom kings seldom undertake wars, and observes that these great agitators of the world, most of them troublers of its peace, are now at rest.

The desolate places they built divide the commentators. Clarke takes them for mausoleums and sepulchral pyramids, raised to keep a name from perishing while the body turns to corruption. Ellicott sharpens the paradox, that gorgeous tombs are desolate precisely because none but the dead tenant them, though he allows the other sense, that places built of old now lie ruined; in the first sense, he thinks, the pyramids may be hinted at. Wesley reads the line differently, of men who to show their wealth or leave a glorious name rebuilt ruined cities, or built new cities and palaces where before there was only solitude and waste.

On the princes with gold the point is what it could not do. Gill notes that their riches lay in metal rather than dominion, that it could not preserve them from death, and that once dead it was no longer theirs. Clarke lets them keep only the empty places prepared for a last dwelling, and closes with a saying from an eastern writer, that nothing satisfies the covetous but the dust that fills his mouth in the grave.
16:
The untimely birth is taken as one more degree of the same wish. Gill notes that the word carries the sense of falling, an abortive being like fruit that drops before it ripens, and that it is called hidden either as hidden in the belly, on one old rendering, or as hidden from sight, having come to no proper shape. Clarke distinguishes two cases in the verse, an early miscarriage scarcely perceptible to the mother, in which the child never had the distinguishable form of a human being at all, and the infants named next, farther advanced but still lost long before their time. Ellicott passes over the detail and states only what the condition would have secured, a release from the experience of suffering; Wesley glosses hidden as undiscerned and unregarded, and adds that the child so described never was in the land of the living.

The grave is then described by what is absent from it. Gill takes the troublers to be those who are like the troubled sea and cannot rest, always devising or doing mischief, and he names three kinds who trouble good men in particular, profane persons by their lives, false teachers by their doctrines, and persecutors by their hard speeches; in the grave, he says, there is neither work nor device, so that men who could not sleep unless they had done mischief now have no power to do any. Clarke reads the verse as a pair of opposites deliberately set against each other, the troubles and the troubled, the restless and the submissive, the toils of the great and the labours of the slave. Ellicott supplies the one thing the verse leaves unsaid, that there means in the grave, the place indicated but never distinctly expressed. Wesley names the oppressors' works as vexations and rapines and murders, and observes that those who were tired out by them now sleep quietly beside them.

On the prisoners the commentators fill in the social detail. Gill thinks of men held for debt, or condemned to the galleys, or in bonds for religion, and makes the point that at death the chains are knocked off and they rest not only with their fellow prisoners but with the men who put them there. Clarke describes slaves who felt all the troubles of life and scarcely tasted any of its pleasures, and says the voice of the oppressor, which was more terrible to them than death, is heard no more. Both he and Ellicott notice that the word for that oppressor is the one rendered taskmaster in the account of the Egyptian bondage, and think the history may be alluded to. Keil and Delitzsch render the line differently again, that the captives dwell together in tranquillity and do not hear the voice of the taskmaster. Wesley adds the limit that keeps the passage honest: Job is not treating here of the state of the dead hereafter, of which he speaks later, but only of their freedom from the troubles of this world, which is the whole matter of the present discourse.

The levelling of small and great is read the same way by all of them and applied differently. Gill takes the pair to cover age and stature and estate together, children and grown men, the mean and the exalted, all arriving without difference and lying without distinction. Clarke calls the grave the appointed place of rendezvous where all these travellers meet, and draws the moral from the shape of a life rather than from its end: equality is absolute at the entrance and at the exit, and the whole intermediate state is disparity, so that the thought should humble the great and the small alike. Wesley turns the same observation into two practical rules, that those who have power should use it moderately and those in subjection should bear it patiently.
20:
That light here means life is agreed; they differ only in what they make of the word. Gill takes it for the light of the living, sweet to a man in health and not to one in pain of body and anguish of mind, who would rather be in the silent grave. Wesley explains why life is called light, since light is pleasant and serviceable for walking and working, and why it is said to be given, since it would be lost were it not daily renewed by a fresh gift. Clarke puts the complaint as a question about fitness, why life is granted to a man incapable of enjoying it or of performing its functions; Ellicott only points to the older connection between life and light elsewhere in Scripture.

Henry reads the verse for what it does not say. The Hebrew runs why doth he give light, without a subject, and Henry observes that Job means God and will not name him, setting this against the adversary's prediction that the man would curse God to his face. He is not indulgent about the rest of it. When men are set on quarrelling there is no end of it, and the corrupt heart will carry on the humour; having cursed the day of his birth Job now courts the day of his death, and the beginning of such impatience is as the letting forth of water. Bitterness of soul, he adds, makes life itself bitter.

The longing for death is described with more sympathy by the others. Gill piles up the verbs, that such men desire and gape for it as a hungry man for his food, and gives the reason it does not come, that the fixed time is not yet; he adds the caution that death is not desirable in itself, being a dissolution of nature and the wages of sin, though good men may lawfully desire it to be free from sinning. Clarke measures the longing by comparison, that they desire separation from life more than men who love gold desire a rich mine. Clarke also reports a manuscript variant which, by the change of a single letter, turns rejoicing with joy into rejoicing at the tomb.

Wesley makes two observations that pull against each other and keeps both. The first is a defence: however earnestly Job dug after death, he never did anything to hasten it, but was content to wait all the days of his appointed time until his change should come. The second is a rebuke: impatience of life on account of its troubles is unnatural and ungrateful to the giver of life, and shows a sinful indulgence of our own passion; the proper care is to get ready for another world and leave God to order the circumstances of the removal.

The man whose way is hidden is described by three of them alike. Clarke takes him for one who knows nothing of what lies before him and is full of fears about both worlds, hedged in so that no way of escape is left; he points to an exact parallel in the Lamentations, where the same complaint is made of being hedged about and the ways enclosed with hewn stone, and declines a conjectural rendering since the common text yields an easy sense already. Wesley says the man does not know which way to turn, and is put as it were in a prison where he can see no possibility of escape. Gill applies it to Job directly, whose way, as he complains, was hidden from the Lord and overlooked, with no regard had to the injuries done him. Ellicott adds the one thing that changes the colour of the verse: this is the same expression used earlier in the book in exactly the opposite sense, where the hedge about the man was why the adversary could not touch him.
24:
The sighing that comes before food is read two ways, and Clarke gives both. The first, which he attributes to an early commentator, takes it of the state of Job's body, so ulcerated that he longed for food but could neither lift it to his mouth nor chew it when it was brought. The second, which Clarke prefers as more natural, is that the sighing took away appetite and served him in place of meat; he sets beside it the psalmist whose tears had been his meat day and night, and remarks that the resemblance is probably not imitation either way but two men describing the same thing. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same sense by the preposition, rendering the line that instead of his food his sighing comes, and noting that the word passes from a local meaning to a substitutionary one as the Latin does. Gill keeps closer to the surface, that there was nothing but sighing before he sat down and tears mingled with the food while he ate, so that these were his meat and drink continually. On the roarings Wesley says they were loud outcries more befitting a lion than a man, poured out with abundance and violence like waters that break their banks, and Clarke compares the noise of a murmuring stream.

What Job feared beforehand is taken by all of them as the point of the verse, and they divide only on its scope. Gill reports one view that the fear was for his children, lest they should sin and bring down judgment, and another that it covered all his troubles, which the changeableness of the world had always led him to expect; on either reading the remark justifies the expostulation, since a man who never had pleasure even in his greatest prosperity may well ask why light is continued to him. Wesley says the same in the first person, that even in prosperity he was full of fears, considering the variety of God's providences and the instability of this vain world, and that those fears are now justified by the event. Ellicott puts the pathos of it more sharply: Job had kept the uncertainty of earthly things always in remembrance, and was overtaken all the same by a calamity that mocked his carefulness and went beyond anything he had apprehended. Clarke turns the admission into a defence. The fear proves that he was not lifted up; he knew that what he had was from Providence and that the giver might take away, and therefore he is not being stripped as a punishment for self-confidence.

The last verse divides Gill and Clarke, and the division is about grammar rather than doctrine. Gill argues that it cannot refer to the time of prosperity at all, since Job was then plainly in safety, God having set a hedge about him so that neither his enemies nor the adversary himself could reach him. Clarke proposes reading the clauses as questions, which yields the opposite sense and an easy one: was I not in safety, had I not rest, had I not comfort, and yet trouble came. He reports a third rendering which makes the point neither of past security nor of past unrest but of speed, that there was no respite as the trouble came on, the evils treading one upon the heels of another; and he compares the psalm where deep calls to deep and all the waves and billows go over the speaker. Wesley takes the verse as a claim about conduct rather than circumstance, that Job had not misbehaved himself in prosperity by presumption or security but had walked humbly and circumspectly, from which he draws the conclusion that in this respect too the man's way was hidden, since he could not see why God should be contending with him.
